prize_parts.citation: for the invention and demonstration of optical lattice atomic clocks, in which atoms confined at a magic wavelength made time measurement possible at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (B053) with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize. Nothing in round 1 weakened the scientific case, and the reservations raised against it are about prize history and timing, not about whether the result is real. A magic-wavelength lattice lets thousands of atoms be interrogated with Doppler and recoil shifts suppressed and with the lattice light shift cancelled to first order. That is a concept and a technique, and it is distinct from the frequency comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012). It has been reproduced at the 1e-18 level by several independent groups and compared across sites, and it has been used for millimetre-scale gravitational redshift tests and constraints on varying constants. That is the independent confirmation and decisive-contribution test I apply to every claim. As Chair I also note that seven of eight members ranked it, and I do not use that as a substitute for the physics. I weigh it on the physics, and on that basis it is the most mature and most cleanly attributable entry on the shortlist. Five members now name it, which tells me the substantive disagreements are narrower than the opening ballots suggested.
statement.case_against: Three reservations remain and I do not dismiss them. First, a reader can see this as the third precision-metrology prize in two decades, with Ye already a 2005 laureate; the answer is that the credited advance is the lattice and its systematics control, but the citation must say so explicitly. Second, the Sr-lattice priority history (Katori's proposal and Tokyo work, Ye's accuracy record, SYRTE, PTB, NIST contributions, Hall, Peik, Hollberg, Lemonde, Ludlow) has not been checked by me against the record, and I am not an atomic physicist. Third, the SI second has not yet been redefined; I regard that as a decision by another body, not a condition on the physics, but it is a real timing argument for those who want a prize tied to a completed outcome. If an expert report found that a third name is necessary, the three-person limit would allow it, but I would then want a convincing justification rather than adding a name for balance.

responses.point: Lindroth asked whether the preference for clean attribution is an argument about tidiness rather than merit, and noted that Lemonde and Ludlow are not credited, while saying B016 would be the natural AMO choice if the committee prefers a new many-body phenomenon over an instrument.
responses.response: I accept her point and do not want tidy credit to decide this. My argument is merit first: independent 1e-18 reproduction and new tests of redshift and constants. Attribution comes second, and there I agree it must be verified. I would ask the expert report specifically whether Lemonde, Ludlow or others have a claim that outranks one of the two names; the limit allows a third name if the record justifies it. On B016, I see Hubbard-model simulation as promising but still a method for answering open questions, with the five credited names too many for the limit, so it does not displace the clocks for me.

responses.point: Eriksson, who prefers B053 in round 1 but lists B033 and B013 as alternatives, says that if the committee prefers discovery of a new quantum state of matter, B033 or B013 would be the better choice and he would not object, and he defers to atomic-physics colleagues on priority.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour, and I take the instrument-versus-phenomenon question as the real fork. I would say it differently from the way it is often put: the lattice clock produced a new regime of measurement, and with it the redshift tests, so it is a physics result and not only an engineering improvement. B033 is eight years old with an unresolved pairing mechanism and Cao outside the names; that is a reason to wait, and I would keep it for a future year. I share his deference on priority and would rely on the same expert report he wants.

responses.point: Olsson prefers aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B052) and defends the statutory word invention, while naming the Krivanek, Dellby and Lupini STEM corrector as an unresolved priority issue.
responses.response: I take the invention argument seriously, and I told her in round 1 that a prize with a clear physics motivation is possible. But her own flag about the STEM corrector is the same kind of attribution problem I raise for the clocks, and unlike the clocks it is not yet answered. By her own argument, a technique prize is acceptable under the statute, and that is also the basis on which I support B053. For me the clocks remain ahead because the independent confirmation and fundamental tests are more extensive, and I would be willing to see B052 reconsidered if an expert report settles the STEM question.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the Higgs experiments (B046), calls attribution the hardest feature, and asks what has been learned about nature from clock tests that are so far null results.
responses.response: On the substance I agree that the Higgs discovery is the stronger single piece of science by the measure of what it tells us about nature, and I keep B046 as my first alternative. But null results are still results: bounds on drift of constants and the redshift tests are quantitative tests of relativity at new precision. The problem for B046 is unchanged, since four founders compete for three places and Danielsson, Johansson and I proposed three different triples. A prize whose citation the committee cannot defend name by name is a prize I would not push, however large the discovery.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers topological insulators (B013) and raises the pending SI redefinition as a reason to wait on the clocks, while arguing the time-reversal Z2 class is distinct from the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I accept that the Z2 insulator class is distinct and that fifteen years of confirmation is solid maturity, so I do not treat B013 as weak. My objection remains attribution: Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan are four names, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe system, and members of this committee already choose different triples. The redefinition does not change the demonstrated clock performance, and a prize that waited for a metrological body's decision would make our judgement depend on theirs. I would be glad to see the expert reports on B013 narrow the names.

uncertainties: Whether expert reports confirm Katori and Ye as the right and sufficient pair, or show that another contributor (for example Lemonde, Ludlow or a SYRTE, PTB or NIST colleague) has a stronger claim.
Whether the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a reason to decline for a majority; I judge it is not, but I cannot demonstrate it.
Whether the pending SI second redefinition should affect timing; I think not, but others disagree.
I have not seen evidence on how members who prefer B046, B013 or B052 would vote if B053 were set aside.
statement.conflict_note: I work in astroparticle physics and detector development (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur), adjacent to IceCube (B009) and the Higgs detector work (B046), neither of which is my preferred part. No conflict is apparent for B053; I have no tie to Katori, Ye or their groups. Kroll's JILA lineage and Lindroth's Lund attosecond ties, which colleagues disclosed, do not change my reading, but I note them as Chair.
